title: The Fighting Irish

jokes.text: Oh, anything that doesn't have the word 'strip,' 'salsa,' or 'beatz' with a Z in the name of it.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Liz what class she wants to take at the gym.
jokes.punchline: She lists three very specific categories to avoid — the specificity of 'beatz with a Z' is the precision punchline.
jokes.explanation: Great character establishment — Liz's neurotic specificity about fitness classes is instantly recognizable. The escalation from 'strip' to 'salsa' to 'beatz with a Z' is well-constructed, with the final beat being the funniest and most specific. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Cardio Hip-Hop Groove it is then.
jokes.setup: Liz has just listed everything she wants to avoid in a class name.
jokes.punchline: Her companion immediately suggests a class that hits several of those notes anyway.
jokes.explanation: A tight callback/ironic reversal. It works because it immediately contradicts Liz's stated preferences with a name that implies exactly those vibes. Economy is near-perfect — four words does all the work.

jokes.text: Nothing, just... going into the same class you're going into.
jokes.setup: Cary runs into Liz (with her boyfriend) at the gym and tries to play it cool.
jokes.punchline: His excuse is transparently false and awkward — he's obviously following her.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the awkwardness of running into a crush while with someone else. The line itself isn't especially clever but the situation generates the laughs.

jokes.text: That's a flower guy.
jokes.setup: Liz's boyfriend introduces her to Cary, apparently the man who sent her flowers, while Cary is clearly interested in her.
jokes.punchline: Liz's sotto voce aside to the audience/camera — 'That's a flower guy' — conveying dawning recognition and mild panic with total economy.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. Three words convey a full comedic situation: awkward triangle, Liz's social anxiety, and a reveal. The deadpan delivery implied by the line is very Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: I did -- actually, I finally just threw them out this morning 'cause they got that really bad flower smell. I kind of couldn't stop smelling them.
jokes.setup: The man who sent Liz flowers asks if she enjoyed them.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a gracious reply, Liz overshares that she threw them out because of the smell — then immediately contradicts herself by saying she couldn't stop smelling them.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Liz Lemon character comedy. The self-contradiction within the same sentence (threw them out / couldn't stop smelling them) captures her inability to function socially in a single beat. The oversharing is deeply in character. Structure is excellent — builds and then immediately undermines itself.

jokes.text: Don't give up, ponytail.
jokes.setup: Liz is clearly struggling in the advanced hip-hop class.
jokes.punchline: Cary encourages her by using 'ponytail' as her name — a gentle, slightly condescending nickname that implies he can't even learn her name but is still into her.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective beat. 'Ponytail' does a lot of work — it's both endearing and slightly objectifying, which adds to the cringe comedy of the situation. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: It's a video of a baby panda... sneezing. Sit here. Don't watch the mother, just watch the baby.
jokes.setup: Jack summons Liz with apparent urgency.
jokes.punchline: It's just to show her a cute baby panda video — then he immediately transitions to firing 10% of her staff. The comedic contrast between the adorable triviality and the brutal corporate news is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structural joke. The setup weaponizes audience trust — we assume Jack's urgency means something important. 'Don't watch the mother, just watch the baby' is the perfect detail that makes Jack seem fully invested in the panda video right before dropping the layoff bombshell. This is quintessential Jack Donaghy — the absurd whiplash between soft/hard, trivial/brutal. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: We're synergizing backward overflow.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz she has to fire 10% of her staff.
jokes.punchline: His corporate justification is pure meaningless jargon — 'synergizing backward overflow' sounds official but is complete nonsense.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy corporate-speak comedy. The phrase sounds just plausible enough to be funny — it has the rhythm of real business jargon while being completely meaningless. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Now, there are 140 people on this show, so go out there and make 126 people very happy.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz she has to fire 10% of her staff of 140.
jokes.punchline: Framing firing 14 people as 'making 126 people very happy' — a darkly optimistic spin that reveals Jack's sociopathic corporate math.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The math is correct (126 = 140 - 14), which makes it more unsettling, and Jack's chipper framing of mass layoffs as a happiness exercise is perfectly in character. Highly quotable. The economy is superb — the whole joke is in that final clause.

jokes.text: Marco. Polo! Marco! Polo! Josh, you suck at this game, man.
jokes.setup: Liz claims everyone on the show is indispensable.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Josh and a crew member playing Marco Polo in what appears to be the studio — two adults playing a children's pool game at work, immediately undermining Liz's claim.
jokes.explanation: Excellent cutaway gag. The structure is perfect — Liz's earnest defense of her team is immediately punctured by evidence that they are, in fact, not indispensable. 'Josh, you suck at this game, man' adds an extra layer of sadness/absurdity. The juxtaposition is the joke.

jokes.text: Getting fired is better than getting killed by my wife. Those big farm people hands crushin' my windpipe.
jokes.setup: Pete dismisses the stress of Liz needing to fire people.
jokes.punchline: His wife's 'big farm people hands' crushing his windpipe is a grotesquely specific image delivered with total nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'big farm people hands' is brilliant. Pete's terrible marriage is a recurring character beat, and this is a great encapsulation of it. Dark, specific, quotable.

jokes.text: Getting fired is better than getting killed by my wife. Those big farm people hands crushin' my windpipe.
jokes.setup: Pete doesn't care about Liz's firing dilemma.
jokes.punchline: His wife killing him with 'big farm people hands' is his greater concern — a hyper-specific, darkly vivid image.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy for Pete. The specificity of 'big farm people hands' is what makes it land — it's not just 'my wife is scary' but a vivid, specific, absurdly detailed fear. Good economy.

jokes.text: You mean that you flat-out lied about getting a vasectomy?
jokes.setup: Pete hints at a 'little secret' about 'Hornberger family planning.'
jokes.punchline: Liz states it bluntly — he lied about a vasectomy — which is both the reveal and the joke.
jokes.explanation: The bluntness is the joke — Pete's euphemism is instantly decoded by Liz in the most direct possible way. Sets up the running gag well.

jokes.text: Do you need a key to my apartment? Just for my own safety.
jokes.setup: Pete is terrified his wife will find out about the vasectomy lie.
jokes.punchline: Liz offers him a safe house key — a joke that reveals her sympathy for Pete's domestic terror while being darkly funny about the severity of his situation.
jokes.explanation: The 'just for my own safety' tag is what elevates this from a straightforward compassionate offer to a joke — it implies Pete genuinely needs asylum. Good economy.

jokes.text: My attorney told me I should join a church preemptively. 'Cause juries are suspicious of celebrities who find religion after getting into trouble.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks Liz where he can find a good church.
jokes.punchline: His reason is purely strategic legal planning — he wants to establish religiosity before his next legal trouble, not spiritual fulfillment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy Jordan character comedy. The premise — pre-emptive church membership as legal strategy — is both absurd and sharply satirical of celebrity justice. The logic is internally coherent (juries ARE suspicious of jailhouse conversions), which makes it funnier. Strong character integration; only Tracy Jordan would think this way and articulate it this clearly.

jokes.text: Why don't you try the Church of Practicology? They love movie stars and stuff.
jokes.setup: Tracy needs a church recommendation.
jokes.punchline: Liz's barely-disguised dig at Scientology — 'Church of Practicology' is a thin pseudonym — and 'they love movie stars and stuff' is a perfect skewering of Scientology's celebrity recruitment.
jokes.explanation: Good satirical bite. The fake name is transparent enough to be funny but the real punchline is 'they love movie stars and stuff' — a perfectly casual takedown of Scientology's celebrity recruitment strategy.

jokes.text: I believe the moon doesn't exist. I believe that vampires are the world's greatest golfers, but their curse is that they'll never get to prove it. I believe that there are 31 letters in the white alphabet.
jokes.setup: Implied context — Tracy is apparently explaining what he said to Scientology auditors that got him rejected.
jokes.punchline: Three escalating absurdist beliefs delivered with total conviction, culminating in the mysterious 'white alphabet' claim.
jokes.explanation: The standout joke of the episode and one of the best Tracy Jordan moments on the show. Three perfectly constructed absurdist beliefs, each funnier than the last. The moon one is solid. The vampire golfer one is brilliant — it has its own internal logic (vampires CAN'T golf in daylight) and 'their curse is that they'll never get to prove it' adds melancholy genius. The 31-letter white alphabet is maximally absurd and mysteriously specific. The 'Wh—what was the question again?' capper is perfect. This is exceptional comedy writing.

jokes.text: Wh--what was the question again?
jokes.setup: Tracy has just listed his three absurdist beliefs.
jokes.punchline: The return to normalcy — Tracy seemingly forgot where the conversation was going — deflates the absurdism perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the absurdist beliefs joke. Its economy is near-perfect — five words — and the implied meaning (Tracy is so far in his own head he lost the thread) is excellent character comedy. Works in tandem with #19.

jokes.text: Mm, I pretty much just do whatever Oprah tells me to.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks Liz what her religion is.
jokes.punchline: Liz reduces her entire spiritual life to following Oprah's advice — a sharp satirical observation about Oprah's cultural authority delivered as sincere self-reflection.
jokes.explanation: Excellent one-liner. It's funny because it's true for a large demographic, it's sharply self-aware of Liz's character (follower, not a spiritual leader), and the delivery is perfectly casual. 'Pretty much' is the right qualifier — it acknowledges the absurdity without winking at it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: And his name is Dona-gee, not Dona-hee.
jokes.setup: Eddie introduces himself as 'Dona-hee' — Jack's brother with a different pronunciation of the family name.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately corrects the pronunciation, establishing the running gag.
jokes.explanation: Sets up an effective running gag about the Donaghy name pronunciation. The payoff comes later; this is the plant.

jokes.text: Eddie Donaghy. As I live and breathe. You're a disgrace! You're not the boss of me, Jack Donaghy! That's Dona-gee, not Dona-hee!
jokes.setup: Jack and Eddie reunite after years apart, moving through affection to insults to a physical fight — mid-fight Jack still corrects pronunciation.
jokes.punchline: Correcting pronunciation during a fistfight is the absurd detail that elevates this from a generic brawl.
jokes.explanation: The pronunciation correction mid-fight is brilliant — it reveals Jack's character (he cannot let go of this even in a brawl) and escalates the running gag perfectly. The rapid swing from 'as I live and breathe' to 'you're a disgrace' in two seconds is also very funny.

jokes.text: You ruined my suit! Aw, shut up, you baby!
jokes.setup: Jack and Eddie are in the middle of a fistfight.
jokes.punchline: Jack's primary concern in a fight is his suit — revealing his material vanity — and Eddie's dismissal as 'baby' is perfectly working-class Irish.
jokes.explanation: Good character integration — Jack's materialist outrage during a brawl is in character. Eddie's retort is appropriately gruff. The suit concern is a reliable Jack character beat.

jokes.text: My dad and Eddie are a blotch on the Dona-hee name--
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to express his shame about his family.
jokes.punchline: He says 'Dona-hee' — the wrong pronunciation — revealing even he sometimes mispronounces his own name.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback execution. Jack getting his own family name wrong in an emotional moment reveals that the Irish family origin says 'Dona-hee' — he's been trying to class up the pronunciation. Perfect setup for the correction.

jokes.text: Dona-gee name.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'Dona-hee' in an emotional moment.
jokes.punchline: Liz's quiet, flat correction mid-scene is perfect — she can't let it go even during a touching moment.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Maximum economy. The joke is entirely in Liz's compulsive need to correct even during emotionally charged moments. The running gag is paying off with increasing precision.

jokes.text: That's how it's pronounced. Say it. Donaghy. Right.
jokes.setup: Liz has just corrected Jack's pronunciation of his own name.
jokes.punchline: Jack insists on the 'correct' pronunciation and makes Liz say it — but the reveal is that Jack IS the one who changed the pronunciation to sound more refined, making Liz the unwitting enforcer of Jack's social climbing.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the mispronunciation arc. Jack's insistence on being corrected (and correcting) reveals his class anxiety — the pronunciation change is his own invention to sound less Irish working-class. Good character depth.

jokes.text: What kind of Presbyterian is this?
jokes.setup: Kenneth has taken Tracy to what appears to be a very enthusiastic, hellfire-style church.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's classification confusion — he expected something mild and got an intense revival — delivered as a sincere question.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the church sequence. Tracy's confusion establishes his religious ignorance entertainingly. The line is economical and in character.

jokes.text: We haven't been Presbyterian for months.
jokes.setup: Tracy asks what kind of Presbyterian this is.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's correction implies the church has gone through multiple denominational phases recently — the throwaway 'for months' suggests rapid religious evolution.
jokes.explanation: A lovely Kenneth line. The implication that a church denomination changes like a fashion trend is absurd and funny, delivered with Kenneth's characteristic earnestness. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Yeah, we lose half the congregation every time American Idol starts up.
jokes.setup: The church meets on Wednesday nights.
jokes.punchline: American Idol competing with church attendance — with half the congregation going to Idol — is a sharp, specific cultural observation delivered with total Kenneth sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Great observational comedy about American popular culture vs. religion. The specificity of American Idol makes it land — it's not just 'TV' but this particular appointment television. Kenneth's deadpan delivery makes it better.

jokes.text: He pointed right at me! He sure did!
jokes.setup: The reverend is delivering a hellfire sermon about sinners.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is convinced the reverend is specifically pointing at him — and Kenneth confirms it enthusiastically.
jokes.explanation: Solid beat. Kenneth's enthusiastic confirmation is the punchline — he sees no irony in confirming his friend is being called out as a sinner. Character comedy for both Tracy (guilt) and Kenneth (obliviousness).

jokes.text: Oh, I forgot your muffin! Banana walnut, your favorite. Uh, that's not correct, but okay.
jokes.setup: The other Liz (Liz Lemler) is being suspiciously nice to Liz Lemon, apparently trying to ingratiate herself.
jokes.punchline: She brings the wrong muffin flavor and claims it's 'your favorite' — Liz Lemon's mild, bewildered correction ('that's not correct, but okay') is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Liz Lemon's polite acceptance of the wrong muffin without real pushback ('that's not correct, but okay') is a nice character beat. The sycophantic behavior from Other Liz sets up later plot mechanics.

jokes.text: Nice hat.
jokes.setup: A staff member arrives with a suspicious quantity of work materials and asks if Liz has heard about layoffs.
jokes.punchline: Liz doesn't answer the question but comments on the hat — implying the hat is part of a transparent 'please don't fire me' costume, and Liz sees right through it.
jokes.explanation: Two-word joke. The implication is everything — the hat is part of an obvious, transparent attempt to be memorable and likeable. Liz's observation without direct comment is perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: You make smart sexy. There's my beautiful boss.
jokes.setup: Multiple staff members are suddenly very nice to Liz as layoff fears spread.
jokes.punchline: The sycophantic compliments are hilariously over the top and transparent.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic montage establishing that everyone is being fake-nice to Liz. 'You make smart sexy' is the standout compliment — absurd enough to be funny.

jokes.text: So your life's a mess, you go out and buy a new suit, pretend everything's okay.
jokes.setup: Eddie is at the NBC building, living at the YMCA, and Jack asks what happened.
jokes.punchline: Eddie accurately diagnoses Jack's (and his own) coping mechanism — a new suit as armor against failure — delivered with working-class bluntness.
jokes.explanation: Insightful character observation. Eddie's reading of Jack through the suit is both psychologically astute and funny as an indictment of Jack's coping mechanisms.

jokes.text: Juvie, Jonestown, that time I punched Goofy. Hell, I even blinded you with a bottle rocket! / I had sex with your prom date. / I stole your identity. / I threw you out of a window. / I convinced you you had lupus. / I microwaved your parakeet. / I hated that bird.
jokes.setup: Eddie is listing all the terrible things he's done to Jack over the years.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from juvenile to genuinely criminal, each item topping the last. Jack's responses minimize or forgive each one, culminating in 'I hated that bird' as a perfect unexpected beat.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. The escalation is masterfully constructed: Juvie → Jonestown → punching Goofy → bottle rocket blinding → prom date → identity theft → window → lupus → microwaved parakeet. Each item is funnier than the last. The Jonestown name-drop and the Goofy specificity are excellent. 'Convinced you you had lupus' is a standout item — creative and specific. The button 'I hated that bird' completely deflates Jack's expected outrage and reveals a surprising depth. This is exceptional escalation comedy writing.

jokes.text: Hmm, you're on my good list, Cary.
jokes.setup: Implied: Cary has done something at work to impress Liz or avoid being fired.
jokes.punchline: Liz's pleased but self-important assessment of Cary — treating her firing power like Santa's naughty/nice list — while clearly also enjoying having power over her love interest.
jokes.explanation: Small but functional beat revealing Liz's power trip. The 'good list' framing is slightly cute, and it advances the Cary storyline.

jokes.text: It's only inappropriate when it's ugly people.
jokes.setup: Liz and Cary are flirting at work. Someone notes it might not be appropriate.
jokes.punchline: Liz's immediate, shameless admission that appearance determines appropriateness rules — a darkly honest insight delivered without shame.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and quotable. It's a cynical-but-true observation about workplace double standards that's delivered by Liz without any self-awareness of her own hypocrisy. The economy is excellent and it's very quotable.

jokes.text: I know who I can fire!
jokes.setup: Liz learns Cary's girlfriend (Other Liz) works in her department.
jokes.punchline: Rather than a professional realization, Liz has a personal, petty epiphany — firing the competition is her solution.
jokes.explanation: A great character beat. Liz's moral flexibility when her own interests are involved is a core character trait, and the joyful exclamation ('I know who I can fire!') is a perfectly calibrated delivery of shameless pettiness.

jokes.text: Good Lord... your eyes. You look like that lady astronaut who tried to kidnap that other woman.
jokes.setup: Pete sees Liz's expression as she hatches her plan.
jokes.punchline: Comparing Liz's obsessive eyes to the Lisa Nowak astronaut/kidnapping incident — a very specific, very recent (2007) news reference — is both a sharp cultural joke and a character observation.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. The Lisa Nowak astronaut reference is brilliantly specific — the 2007 story of an astronaut driving across the country in adult diapers to confront a romantic rival was exactly this kind of obsessive, jealous, woman-vs-woman story. Pete connecting Liz's jealous eyes to that story is both very funny and perfectly appropriate. The 'good lord' setup builds the moment well.

jokes.text: Diapers, Mace, Houston to Orlando in nine hours? Blammo.
jokes.setup: Pete has compared Liz to the astronaut kidnapper.
jokes.punchline: Rather than being offended, Liz admires the astronaut's efficiency and planning — 'Blammo' as a seal of approval on a kidnapping plot is darkly hilarious and reveals her own obsessive state.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The subversion is total — Liz isn't embarrassed by the comparison, she's inspired by it. 'Diapers, Mace, Houston to Orlando in nine hours? Blammo.' is a perfectly constructed sentence: the items enumerate the plan, 'nine hours' is the impressive detail, and 'Blammo' is an insane sign-off. The character integration is exceptional — Liz's admiration for competence in any domain, even obsessive kidnapping, is perfectly in character. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I know I'm the guy who lied to his wife about having a vasectomy, but this... this is wrong.
jokes.setup: Pete objects to Liz's plan to sabotage the other Liz.
jokes.punchline: Pete's moral objection is undermined by his own confession — the guy who has a fake vasectomy is the voice of ethical reason.
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the callback to the vasectomy lie, (2) the irony of Pete being the moral authority, (3) the implication that whatever Liz is doing is worse than lying to your wife about a vasectomy. The self-awareness in 'I know I'm the guy who...' is perfect. Highly quotable as a template ('I know I'm the guy who X, but this is wrong').

jokes.text: Jack is out of my hair, people are being nice to me. There's a guy I like in the building, and I have the authority to fire his girlfriend?
jokes.setup: Liz justifies her corrupt plan.
jokes.punchline: The increasingly petty list of good fortune culminates in 'I have the authority to fire his girlfriend' delivered as if it's a natural extension of good luck — which reveals how far she's gone.
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Liz's self-justification list is a window into her rationalizing mind. The escalation from legitimate good things to 'authority to fire his girlfriend' is the structure.

jokes.text: For the first time ever, things are lining up for old Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: Liz has been justifying her corrupt use of firing power.
jokes.punchline: The self-pitying 'for the first time ever' combined with the third-person 'old Liz Lemon' is both funny and sad — a catchphrase being born.
jokes.explanation: The introduction of a running phrase for this episode. 'Old Liz Lemon' third-person reference is a great character tic — self-deprecating, slightly pathetic, but also triumphant. The catchphrase quality is high; it recurs and pays off beautifully later.

jokes.text: Hey, Jack, uh, you mind if I take a few grapes for dinner later?
jokes.setup: Eddie and Jack have had an emotional family reunion scene.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's request to take a few grapes for dinner reveals his poverty/homelessness with gentle humor — it's played with dignity but the implication is heartbreaking and funny simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Understated and effective. The tragedy-comedy blend is well-calibrated. Eddie's dignity in asking for grapes is both funny and sad. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: They never once said anything about the racist stuff towards the end.
jokes.setup: Eddie asks Jack to donate to the nurses who took care of their father.
jokes.punchline: The casual aside that their father became racist at the end — and that the nurses' professionalism is being praised for tolerating it — is darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The construction is perfect — it's buried as a subordinate clause in what's ostensibly a touching request. The qualifier 'towards the end' suggests it started at some point, which makes it worse. The nurses are being praised for tolerating racism, which is a darkly real situation delivered as a throwaway. Sharp writing.

jokes.text: But you had to go to the bathroom, so Dad missed seeing Meredith Vieira! Now I'm pissed!
jokes.setup: The Donaghy siblings are sharing memories of their father.
jokes.punchline: A deeply petty grievance — that a bathroom break caused their father to miss seeing Meredith Vieira — suddenly erupting into rage at a sibling reunion.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully absurd family grievance comedy. The specificity of 'Meredith Vieira' (not just 'the TV') elevates it. The rage over such a trivial slight at a mourning family gathering is both realistic and absurd. The 'Now I'm pissed!' escalation is perfect.

jokes.text: Not one of you kids is ever gonna amount to anything. That's why your mom left.
characters: One of the Donaghy siblings (quoting their father)
jokes.setup: Someone mentions their father was 'always ready with a joke.'
jokes.punchline: His idea of a joke is predicting his children's failure and blaming them for their mother leaving — which apparently counted as humor in the Donaghy household.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy that reveals Jack's character origins. The setup ('he was always ready with a joke') creates an expectation of warmth, which is perfectly subverted by the cruelty of the actual 'joke.' The two-punch structure (failure prediction + mom leaving) escalates well.

jokes.text: Maybe we should get all the Donaghy kids back together again. Aw, Jack, they don't wanna see me. Oh, come on, we're Irish. We're a forgiving people.
jokes.setup: Jack wants to reunite the family.
jokes.punchline: Jack's confident assertion that 'we're Irish, we're a forgiving people' is immediately ironic given the Donaghy siblings' combative behavior throughout the episode.
jokes.explanation: Solid ironic joke — the episode has established the Donaghys as specifically not a forgiving people, making Jack's cultural pride funny.

jokes.text: Kabbalah is a wonderful religion that mixes the fun part of Judaism with magic.
jokes.setup: Tracy is still on his religion quest and has found a new option.
jokes.punchline: His description of Kabbalah — 'the fun part of Judaism with magic' — is reductive and absurd but not entirely wrong, which makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The economy of 'the fun part of Judaism with magic' is excellent. Tracy's sincere, reductive summaries of religions are a good running bit throughout this episode.

jokes.text: This one sounds really expensive and gay.
jokes.setup: Tracy is pitching Kabbalah to Eddie.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's blunt, classist-and-homophobic two-word summary of Kabbalah perfectly captures his working-class Irish Catholic worldview.
jokes.explanation: Economy is exceptional — two adjectives do everything. It's a very character-specific line for Eddie: the class judgment ('expensive') and the cultural conservatism ('gay') are perfect for a working-class Boston Irish Catholic. The observation about Kabbalah being celebrity-expensive is also accurate.

jokes.text: Now, I know there's been a lot of controversy around the church lately. You know, because of The Da Vinci Code.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining Irish Catholicism to Eddie.
jokes.punchline: Jack cites The Da Vinci Code (a fictional novel) as the source of 'controversy around the church' rather than the actual abuse scandals — a darkly funny misdirection about what Jack considers the real PR problem for Catholicism.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The Catholic abuse scandal is the elephant in the room that Jack's character studiously avoids by citing a Dan Brown novel instead. The misdirection is technically perfect — 'a lot of controversy' sets up expectation of the real scandal, and 'The Da Vinci Code' is the perfectly absurd substitution. Deeply in character for Jack (Catholic apologist, corporate spin master). Highly quotable. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: I'm Irish Catholic.
jokes.setup: Jack has been explaining Irish Catholicism to Eddie, including the confession benefit.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's simple 'I'm Irish Catholic' — delivered after Jack's pitch — as if he needed to be sold on his own lifelong religion.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button. The joke is structural — Jack selling his own religion to his own brother, who already has it. Three words of maximum economy.

jokes.text: Played saxophone in the marching band at Rutgers? Kept that a secret from your employer, didn't you?
jokes.setup: Liz has 'gathered information' on Other Liz as part of her plan.
jokes.punchline: The most damning secret Liz could find on Other Liz is that she played saxophone in the marching band at Rutgers — a completely harmless fact that Liz treats like a scandal.
jokes.explanation: Good joke about Liz's desperate, misguided 'plan.' The specificity of saxophone (not trumpet, not tuba) and Rutgers (not a prestigious school) is perfect. Treating a marching band membership as a career-ending secret is the right level of Liz absurdity.

jokes.text: Heart of gold, L.L. Is there a limit to how much we can give? I hope not. Let's get our checkbooks! Yeah!
jokes.setup: Eddie has set up a charity collection jar for the hospital that cared for their father.
jokes.punchline: The Donaghy family immediately becomes enthusiastically generous — which is a setup for the reveal that 'C.A.S.H.' is a scam (visible in retrospect).
jokes.explanation: This scene functions primarily as setup for the C.A.S.H. reveal — the comedy is in retrospect once we know they're being scammed. The scene itself is moderately funny on first viewing.

jokes.text: I bet Pops is looking down right now and saying, 'If I could come back and do any broad, it'd be that one right there.'
jokes.setup: The family is having a touching moment about their father.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's idea of a touching posthumous tribute from their father is a crude sexual fantasy — perfectly calibrated to the kind of father established earlier.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the father's character is excellent — we already know he told cruel 'jokes,' so a crude posthumous thought attributed to him fits perfectly. The construction ('looking down and saying...') sets up a sentimental eulogy expectation that's perfectly subverted. 'That one right there' is the right trashy specificity.

jokes.text: Ew.
jokes.setup: Eddie has just attributed a crude sexual thought to their dead father.
jokes.punchline: Liz's single-word reaction is the perfect response — disgust without excess.
jokes.explanation: A simple but well-placed reaction beat. 'Ew' is maximally economical and Liz Lemon's squeamishness in the face of crude behavior is very in character.

jokes.text: This is, uh, Margaret. We just found out about her today.
jokes.setup: Jack is introducing his family members to Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: The casual revelation of a previously unknown sibling is delivered as if it's a mildly interesting footnote to a family reunion.
jokes.explanation: Strong understatement comedy. The revelation of an unknown sibling is a major family bombshell, but Jack's tone ('we just found out about her today') treats it as entirely routine. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Well, we've been toasting Pop for over an hour now. Maybe we should pace ourselves.
jokes.setup: Someone wants to make another toast to Pop.
jokes.punchline: Jack's concern about pacing their drinking at an Irish wake is both sensible and reveals the absurdity of Irish funeral culture — one hour of toasts and they haven't finished.
jokes.explanation: Solid Irish-drinking stereotype joke that's specific enough (over an hour of consecutive toasts) to be more than a generic observation.

jokes.text: Come here, you magnificent douche bag!
jokes.setup: Eddie arrives at the family gathering.
jokes.punchline: The greeting 'you magnificent douche bag' is an expression of pure Donaghy family affection — insult as endearment, delivered with warmth.
jokes.explanation: Great character moment for the Donaghy family. 'Magnificent' + 'douche bag' is the right paradox — pride and insult together. It tells you everything about this family's emotional register.

jokes.text: Stop showing off and have a drink.
jokes.setup: Eddie mentions he's been clean and sober for seven months.
jokes.punchline: Treating sobriety as 'showing off' and pressuring him to drink is a perfectly observed Irish family dysfunction moment delivered as if it's reasonable.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Stop showing off and have a drink' is a perfect encapsulation of Irish drinking culture's relationship with sobriety. The deadpan delivery implies this is a reasonable position. The callback-to-tragedy element (he caves immediately — 'Sure') deepens the comedy. Highly quotable and very true.

jokes.text: What would you say are your weaknesses? Some people say I'm too nice.
jokes.setup: Liz is conducting a fake performance review on the other Liz as part of her scheme.
jokes.punchline: Other Liz gives the most clichéd job interview answer ('some people say I'm too nice') — which is both a parody of bad interview answers and a beat that makes her sympathetic.
jokes.explanation: The 'too nice' weakness answer is a well-worn trope but functions here as character comedy (Other Liz is a generic nice person in contrast to Liz Lemon's chaos).

jokes.text: Well, hopefully, I'll still be working for G.E. It's a great company for working moms. What? You know, in five years. In--I mean, I'm in a relationship right now. By then I'll probably have a couple of kids, be living in the suburbs -- just having it all, really.
jokes.setup: Liz asks 'Where do you see yourself in five years?' as part of her fake performance review scheme.
jokes.punchline: Other Liz's perfectly normative life plan (working mom, suburbs, 'having it all') is the exact opposite of Liz Lemon's chaotic singleton existence — and it triggers Liz's immediate nuclear response.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed cringe comedy. Other Liz's answer is the setup; the joke is Liz Lemon's reaction. The 'having it all, really' is the final nail — completely ordinary ambition that Liz finds threatening. Sets up the perfect punchline.

jokes.text: You're fired! I'm the decider!
jokes.setup: Other Liz describes a normal, happy future life.
jokes.punchline: Liz fires her on the spot — and 'I'm the decider' references George W. Bush's infamous 2006 press conference quote, delivered with maximum conviction.
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm the decider' Bush reference is perfectly placed — it makes Liz's petty power exercise feel grandiose and absurd simultaneously. The timing of the firing (immediately after 'having it all, really') is excellent structure.

jokes.text: It's too bad it took Dad dying to get us all together again. He was always bringing people together. He was just like Lady Di.
jokes.setup: The family reflects on their father's passing.
jokes.punchline: Comparing their abusive, crude, racist father to Lady Diana is the most absurd possible comparison — delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The Lady Di comparison works because we've already heard what this father was like (racist, cruel 'jokes,' abandoned by wife). The contrast is the joke. Good absurdist character comedy.

jokes.text: To Pop! The sorriest bastard that ever walked the earth.
jokes.setup: The family makes toasts to Pop at the reunion.
jokes.punchline: Eddie's heartfelt toast descriptor — 'the sorriest bastard that ever walked the earth' — is delivered as if it's a loving tribute, which is both funny and characterizes the Donaghy family perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy toast that fits perfectly with the Donaghy family's emotional register. Insult-as-affection again, but it works.

jokes.text: Seriously, don't even start with me! Don't start with me, Mrs.!
jokes.setup: The family confrontation is continuing to escalate after Eddie's toast.
jokes.punchline: The rapid-fire arguing with overlapping 'don't start with me' volleys is the joke — the Donaghy family in full chaos, with Jack's 'forgiving people' claim completely destroyed.
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation beat but not particularly original on its own. The comedy comes from context — the contrast with Jack's 'forgiving people' claim — rather than the dialogue itself.

jokes.text: No, no, you're not! You're fired! Did you just fire Pete? Yes! I'm gonna put his name on a list! And everything!
jokes.setup: Liz has fired Other Liz; Pete objects and threatens to go to HR.
jokes.punchline: Liz fires Pete for objecting to the firing, then descends into increasingly unhinged assertions of power ('I'm gonna put his name on a list! And everything!').
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation comedy. The 'I'm gonna put his name on a list! And everything!' is a brilliant detail — 'and everything' implies Liz's power trip has outpaced her actual ability to articulate consequences. The comic rhythm is perfect.

jokes.text: Ms. Lemon, the accounting department wishes to protest the firing of our colleague. Now, we have discussed it-- You're fired! You're all fired! Clean out your desks! Fired!
jokes.setup: The accounting department sends a formal representative to protest.
jokes.punchline: Liz fires all of them the moment they try to speak, cutting off the representative mid-sentence with maximum efficiency.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation with perfect structure. The representative is cut off mid-sentence — Liz has fully lost control. Firing an entire department for protesting a firing is beautifully absurd. The staccato delivery of 'Fired! / Clean out your desks! / Fired!' is great comic rhythm.

jokes.text: And if I don't have any accountants--
jokes.setup: Jack explains why firing accountants is a problem.
jokes.punchline: Jack trailing off — allowing Liz to complete the implication herself — is the joke. The absurdity of having no accountants is so obvious he doesn't need to finish.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat. The trailing off is appropriately deadpan but the joke itself isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: Lemon, is this about a boy?
jokes.setup: Liz claims she had 'a plan' for the firings.
jokes.punchline: Jack's immediate, accurate read — 'is this about a boy?' — cuts through all of Liz's rationalization with devastating simplicity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jack Donaghy line. His ability to see through Liz's chaos to its embarrassingly simple emotional core is a running dynamic that works every time. 'Is this about a boy?' delivered as if he's very slightly disappointed is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Flower guy? Lemon, you've gone chicken killer on me over a guy whose name you don't know?
jokes.setup: Liz confirms it's about Cary (the flower guy).
jokes.punchline: 'Chicken killer' as Jack's term for Liz's obsessive descent (presumably a reference to the astronaut story or another cultural reference) plus the devastating observation that she doesn't even know his name.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback construction. 'Chicken killer' is a vivid, specific phrase (tying back to the astronaut/obsession thread) and the 'guy whose name you don't know' twist drives the knife in perfectly — all of this chaos for someone Liz can only call 'flower guy.' The economy and character integration are both very strong.

jokes.text: That's...very sad.
jokes.setup: Liz defends herself: 'He just seems like a really cool guy, and I think he likes me more than her.'
jokes.punchline: Jack's devastatingly simple three-word assessment.
jokes.explanation: Three words of brutal deadpan. Jack's blunt empathy (he is genuinely sad for Liz but can't disguise the comedy of her situation) is perfect Jack characterization. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Eddie just said to write the initials on the check. C... A... S... H.
jokes.setup: Liz is writing a check to 'Chicago All Saints Hospital' for Eddie's charity.
jokes.punchline: She spells out C-A-S-H and it dawns on her (and the audience) that Eddie has set up a scam where checks are written out to 'CASH.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The joke is set up earlier with the enthusiastic donation scene and pays off here. The slow, dawning realization as Liz spells out C-A-S-H is well-paced — the audience figures it out one letter before she does. The 'Son of a bitch' punchline lands perfectly. Well-crafted long-form misdirection.

jokes.text: Son of a bitch.
jokes.setup: Liz has realized the charity 'C.A.S.H.' is a scam.
jokes.punchline: The single expletive is the perfect reaction — admiration and frustration in equal measure.
jokes.explanation: The button on the CASH reveal. Works as a reaction beat — the tone could be horror or grudging admiration. Economy is perfect (three words). The reveal earns this reaction.

jokes.text: Eddie already took the other box.
jokes.setup: Liz has just realized the CASH scam.
jokes.punchline: There was already another donation box — Eddie ran the scam twice. The casual delivery of this escalation is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation. Learning that Eddie already ran the scam once before and took those proceeds too is a great deepening of the joke. The economy is near-perfect; the understatement of the delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Your brother Eddie's dead. He wanted you to have his watch.
jokes.setup: Jack has just learned his father died — now a second 'Eddie' appears pulling the same Dead Man's Curve con.
jokes.punchline: The exact same scam (dead relative + watch) is being run again, this time with the real Eddie as the 'dead' person.
jokes.explanation: Great structural callback — the same con being run on the same mark by a different family member reveals the scope of the Donaghy family grift enterprise. The watch is the recurring prop that ties it together.

jokes.text: I'm pulling the Dead Man's Curve on Jack. When we parted ways, we agreed that I would get Jack and you would do the thing in Sacramento!
jokes.setup: Two unknown Donaghys are revealed to both be running scams on Jack simultaneously.
jokes.punchline: There is a coordinated Donaghy family con operation with Jack as the shared mark — and they're arguing about territorial rights to him.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jack's whole family is a professional con operation targeting him is a brilliant escalation. The territorial dispute between family con artists ('you would do the thing in Sacramento') is darkly funny and deeply original. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: You are both a disgrace to the Donaghy name! It's pronounced Dona-fee, you lace curtain half-an-Englishman!
jokes.setup: Two Donaghys are fighting over their con territory.
jokes.punchline: A third previously unknown Donaghy appears and — in the ultimate evolution of the name pronunciation gag — introduces yet another pronunciation ('Dona-fee') while calling the others 'lace curtain half-an-Englishman.'
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff of the episode's running pronunciation gag. Each iteration has added a layer: first Liz correcting Eddie, then Jack mispronouncing his own name, then Liz correcting Jack, then Jack enforcing the 'correct' version — and now a third pronunciation appears ('Dona-fee') suggesting Jack's 'Dona-gee' is itself a class-aspirational invention. 'Lace curtain half-an-Englishman' is beautifully specific Irish class-hierarchy invective. Exceptional running gag resolution.

jokes.text: When I think of all the things that I've been holding inside me that I wanted to say to you... Well, now I'm gonna let St. Patrick and St. Michael do my talking for me! You'll have to get through Tip O'Neill and Bobby Sands first!
jokes.setup: Two Donaghys are about to fight.
jokes.punchline: They name their fists after Irish Catholic/political figures — St. Patrick, St. Michael, Tip O'Neill, Bobby Sands — an absurdist escalation of the Irish identity theme.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist comedy. Named fists are already a great comedic device; named after Irish Catholic saints and hunger-strike martyrs takes it to another level. 'Tip O'Neill and Bobby Sands' is a perfect pair — the contrast between the jolly Speaker of the House and the IRA hunger striker is inspired.

jokes.text: You call those fist names? Say hello to Bono and Sandra Day O'Connor!
jokes.setup: The first pair have named their fists after Irish/Irish-American icons.
jokes.punchline: Bono and Sandra Day O'Connor as fist names — a wildly mismatched pair (Irish rock star vs. American jurist) delivered with maximum conviction.
jokes.explanation: The funniest of the named fists jokes. 'Sandra Day O'Connor' as a fist name is brilliantly incongruous — she's an 87-year-old Supreme Court justice. The pairing with Bono (slightly more explicable as an Irish icon) makes it funnier. 'Those are the stupidest fist names I've ever heard' is the perfect button. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: Those are the stupidest fist names I've ever heard.
jokes.setup: Bono and Sandra Day O'Connor are offered as fist names.
jokes.punchline: An objective assessment that also implies the other fist names were BETTER, which is itself absurd.
jokes.explanation: A great button that plays both ways — judging Sandra Day O'Connor as a bad fist name while implicitly endorsing Bobby Sands and Tip O'Neill as reasonable ones. The implication that there's a GOOD standard for fist names is the joke.

jokes.text: I want you... to punch your sister in the face.
jokes.setup: Liz says she's okay after the brawl and Jack asks what she needs.
jokes.punchline: Jack's solution to the Donaghy family chaos is not de-escalation but specific, targeted violence — 'punch your sister in the face' — delivered as a measured tactical decision.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The pause before 'to punch your sister in the face' builds anticipation perfectly, and the precision of 'your sister' (not a random target) makes it funnier. Jack has apparently done strategic family violence triage and concluded this is the correct move. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: It's on. I call same sides as the bicentennial brawl!
jokes.setup: Jack says it's on (the family fight).
jokes.punchline: The casual reference to a 'bicentennial brawl' — implying the Donaghys have a recurring family brawl tradition going back to 1976 with established team assignments — is gloriously absurd.
jokes.explanation: The 'bicentennial brawl' detail is excellent — it implies a recurring tradition of family violence with organized team sides. '1976' specificity is the right level of absurdist commitment. The fact that there are established SIDES implies this has happened multiple times with consistent alignment.

jokes.text: I was impressed by how you take a punch, Lemon. I played dead for the worst of it, but it didn't fool your family.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz are in the aftermath of the Donaghy family brawl.
jokes.punchline: Jack played dead to avoid fighting — and the Donaghys continued punching him anyway because they could tell he wasn't actually dead.
jokes.explanation: Excellent post-fight recap comedy. Two great details: (1) Jack's tactical choice to play dead in a fight, which is very in character for Jack (strategic even in chaos), and (2) the Donaghys not being fooled — implying they have experience with this tactic. 'Impressed by how you take a punch, Lemon' is also a very good character moment.

jokes.text: To know that they'll be there after I'm dead, fighting over my corpse before it's cryogenically frozen.
jokes.setup: Jack says the family brawl was 'strangely reassuring.'
jokes.punchline: Jack has planned to be cryogenically frozen after death — and apparently the family already knows and plans to fight over the corpse before it happens.
jokes.explanation: Great character detail. The cryogenic freezing is the unexpected specificity that makes it funny — Jack has a detailed post-death plan and assumes his family will attempt to interfere with it. The matter-of-fact delivery is excellent.

jokes.text: I gave him and my dad a three-day head start out of love and sportsmanship.
jokes.setup: Liz asks where Eddie is now after the con was revealed.
jokes.punchline: Jack gave his scam-artist father and brother a three-day head start before presumably reporting them — and frames this as 'love and sportsmanship,' as if it's a foxhunt.
jokes.explanation: One of Jack's best lines in the episode. 'Out of love and sportsmanship' is a perfect combination — the first word ('love') is genuine, and the second ('sportsmanship') makes it absurd, as if pursuing his criminal family is a game with fair-play conventions. The three-day specificity is right. Highly quotable. Earns its 8+ rating.

jokes.text: As always, it's been a pleasure fighting with you.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz conclude their conversation after the Donaghy family chaos.
jokes.punchline: 'Fighting with you' can mean both literal fighting (the brawl) and the ongoing workplace struggle between them — Jack says it as a genuine compliment.
jokes.explanation: Nice double-meaning line that characterizes Jack and Liz's relationship. The warmth is genuine and the wordplay is efficient.

jokes.text: Oh, I had to rehire that Liz Lemler that you fired. / And I didn't want any more trouble with her, so I had to give her a promotion too. / It's an amazing opportunity for her out at, uh, corporate headquarters. / In Connecticut?
jokes.setup: Jack reveals the consequences of Liz's firing spree.
jokes.punchline: Each sentence escalates: rehire → promotion → corporate headquarters → Connecticut. Liz's dawning horror as each detail lands is the comedy. Connecticut is the comic nadir — a fate worse than firing.
jokes.explanation: Strong escalating reveal. The joke builds with each line — each 'consequence' is worse than the last from Liz's perspective. 'Connecticut?' as the punch is sharp — within the New York TV world, corporate Connecticut is the anti-paradise.

jokes.text: It seems that things are lining up once again for old Liz Lemon.
jokes.setup: Jack reveals that the other Liz has been transferred to Connecticut.
jokes.punchline: Jack adopts Liz's own catchphrase from earlier — 'things are lining up for old Liz Lemon' — to announce the outcome, perfectly completing the arc.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Jack using Liz's own self-pitying catchphrase to deliver good news is deeply satisfying structurally. It reveals Jack paid attention to Liz's emotional state and is now solving her problem with his characteristic elegant manipulation. The irony that Liz's chaos produced the desired outcome is the final twist. Strong episode-closing joke.

jokes.text: I hear your girlfriend got transferred. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Liz runs into Cary and delivers condolences about his girlfriend's transfer.
jokes.punchline: Liz is the one who caused the transfer and is now offering fake sympathy — the irony is total.
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Liz delivering condolences for damage she caused. The 'Sorry' is perfectly hypocritical. The scene is also a comeuppance (Cary isn't interested in Liz once his girlfriend is gone).

jokes.text: You forgot to give me the key to your place, and I need it, my wife knows about our little secret.
jokes.setup: Pete appears while Liz is talking to Cary.
jokes.punchline: Pete's vasectomy situation has exploded — the 'little secret' has been discovered — and he's calling in the apartment key offer from earlier.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff for the vasectomy plot. Pete's life has predictably collapsed and the apartment key offer is being called in — confirms the earlier dark joke. The timing (during Liz's moment with Cary) is good comedic structure.

jokes.text: Oh, God. I should've just gotten a vasectomy!
jokes.setup: Pete's wife has found out about the fake vasectomy.
jokes.punchline: Pete's belated realization — delivered as genuine regret — that actually getting the vasectomy would have been the simpler solution.
jokes.explanation: The logical endpoint of the vasectomy arc. Pete's regret is funny because it's completely obvious and comes too late. 'I should've just gotten a vasectomy' as a life lesson is highly quotable.

jokes.text: I'm IrisCatholic now. Like you, Regis, and the Pope.
jokes.setup: Tracy has converted to Irish Catholicism after the church scenes.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's identification of Jack's fellow Irish Catholics as 'you, Regis, and the Pope' — grouping Jack Donaghy with Regis Philbin and the Pope as a peer group — is perfectly absurdist.
jokes.explanation: Great Tracy line. Grouping Jack Donaghy with Regis Philbin and the Pope as a peer set is genuinely funny — Regis is the perfect 'one of these things is not like the others' addition. Also 'IrisCatholic' as one word is a nice character touch.

jokes.text: Oh, no, you're not. The church already has enough lawsuits.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces he's now Irish Catholic.
jokes.punchline: Jack's rejection cites the church's existing lawsuit burden — a darkly frank acknowledgment of the Catholic abuse scandal that he avoided directly addressing earlier (Da Vinci Code joke).
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback — Jack finally addresses the actual Catholic scandal (lawsuits) having avoided it earlier with the Da Vinci Code misdirection. His concern is characteristically corporate (liability) rather than moral. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: See, I could screw up now, and then just go to confession. No longer do I have to throw my parties in international waters.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains the appeal of the confession loophole.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has been throwing parties in international waters to avoid U.S. law — confession as a preferable alternative to maritime law parties is a gloriously absurd character detail.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'No longer do I have to throw my parties in international waters' is a perfect Tracy Jordan line — it reveals that his parties have been so illegal that they required maritime jurisdiction to conduct, and that he considers this a significant inconvenience. The logic is internally coherent (international waters = no U.S. law) which makes it funnier. The casual delivery as if this is a normal consideration is exceptional character comedy. Earns its 9.

jokes.text: Whether things are good, or bad, or you're simply eating tacos in the park. There is always the crushing guilt.
jokes.setup: Jack explains that Catholicism involves crushing guilt even in good times.
jokes.punchline: 'Eating tacos in the park' as the example of a guilt-free activity that Catholicism nevertheless makes guilty is the perfect specific detail — innocuous, pleasant, and suddenly burdened with sin.
jokes.explanation: Excellent observational comedy about Catholic guilt. The escalation from 'good' to 'bad' to 'eating tacos in the park' is perfect — the third term is the joke, and 'tacos in the park' is specifically innocuous enough to be funny. Jack's earnest delivery of this as a selling point (or at least honest disclosure) is great character comedy. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I don't think I want that. I'm out. Somehow I feel oddly guilty about that. I don't want nothing crushing me.
jokes.setup: Jack describes the crushing guilt of Catholicism.
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately opts out — then immediately feels guilty about opting out — perfectly proving Jack's point about Catholic guilt being inescapable, even for non-Catholics.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. The structure is airtight: Tracy opts out of a religion to avoid guilt, immediately feels guilty, which proves the thing he was trying to avoid. 'I don't want nothing crushing me' is the perfect Tracy button. The meta-joke is that simply learning about Catholic guilt infected him with it. Exceptional payoff for the Tracy/religion subplot.

tmdb_overview: Jack helps his brother Eddie land a job at 'TGS', Liz is forced to make desperate staff cutbacks, and Tracy seeks spiritual fulfillment with help from Kenneth.
insight: Observational dark comedy sustains 89-point rating across 59 jokes in 22 minutes.
